description: Hi! For this hackathon, we aim to build "PyroSync" — an explainable, data-driven platform that unifies 20+ years of multi-sensor satellite fire hotspots into a standardized burning activity calendar and early-warning dashboard.
summary: PyroSync is a web app that turns 20+ years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see the same fires differently: gluing their raw counts together makes every year since 2012 look about 5.1× more fiery. We count fire cell-days on a common ~1 km grid and calibrate VIIRS to the MODIS Aqua scale using the years both flew (2012–2020), chaining NOAA-20 through Suomi NPP after its data stopped in November 2026. On held-out years, monthly error falls from over 500% to about 19%, with total bias under 1%. Users pick an area, see which months and years burned most, and compare any month with its historical median, with uncertainty ranges and CSV downloads. Our Indonesia case study answers a question Malaysians asked during October’s haze: 2026 is Indonesia’s worst fire season since 2015, but not a record.
details:
Project Summary

PyroSync is a free web app that turns more than 20 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see the same fires very differently, so their raw counts cannot be joined. PyroSync converts VIIRS onto the MODIS Aqua scale, so the fire record runs from 2003 to today without a false jump when the satellites change.

Users pick an area, either a province preset or their own latitude/longitude rectangle. They then see which months and years burned most, how any month compares with its historical median, and how the current fire season ranks. Every number carries an uncertainty range, and all results can be downloaded as CSV.

Our case study answers the question Malaysians asked during October 2026, when smoke from Indonesian fires reached Malaysia: is this the worst fire year ever?

  • Live app: https://pyrosync.streamlit.app (if the app is asleep, click the wake-up button and wait about a minute)
  • Code (GitHub): https://github.com/QingLTC/pyrosync
  • Slide (global judges, 7 pages): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EZbiGjXXcH7m3Cyuzyoi6B7tIN9KlB_w/view?usp=sharing
  • Demo video (local judges, up to 3 min): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1osbod1X2GVbZ1CPw9rxyicd3JQQpN82I/view?usp=drive_link

How We Addressed the Challenge

The problem. MODIS uses 1 km pixels; VIIRS uses 375 m pixels. VIIRS detects smaller and cooler fires and splits one fire into several pixels. Over 2012–2020, VIIRS logged 5.1× as many detections as MODIS for the same area. Gluing the two records together invents a five-fold jump in 2012. As MODIS retires, every future year would look like a record.

Our solution, in six steps:

  1. Clean. Keep only good-quality detections, and remove static heat sources (volcanoes, smelters, gas flares) that are not vegetation fires.
  2. Use a common unit. Count fire cell-days, meaning a ~1 km grid cell with at least one hotspot on a given day, per sensor and per day/night pass. This removes most of the “one fire = many VIIRS pixels” effect.
  3. Calibrate (Layer A). Learn the ratio of MODIS Aqua to VIIRS cell-days separately for each region, calendar month and day/night pass. We use 2012–2020, when both satellites passed at about 13:30 local time and before Aqua’s orbit began to drift. Resampling whole years gives a 5–95% uncertainty range.
  4. Chain the sensors. Suomi NPP stopped delivering FIRMS data on 2 November 2026, so NOAA-20 is aligned to Suomi NPP first, then to the Aqua scale.
  5. Check with machine learning (Layer B). A gradient-boosted Poisson regression predicts Aqua cell-days from VIIRS features (counts, fire radiative power, share of low-intensity fires, month, region, location).
  6. Build the calendar. MODIS Aqua is used up to 2020 and harmonized VIIRS from 2021.

Validation. We trained on 2012–2017 and tested on 2018–2020 against real MODIS Aqua for Indonesia. Monthly error fell from 501% (raw VIIRS cell-days) to 18.9%, with a total bias of only +0.7%. The machine-learning model scored 23.0%, no better than the simple ratio. We therefore made the transparent ratio the default.

Testing our own pipeline. Our first static-source filter removed 13% of all detections. A diagnostic showed the removed “vegetation fire” detections were as seasonal as real fires (65% in August–October, against 69% overall), so we were deleting real fires near industrial sites. The revised filter removes about 7%, and calibration bias dropped from +4.5% to +0.7%.

Results: Indonesia, 2026. The August–October 2026 fire season totals 53,697 fire cell-days (range 46,771–58,307). That makes it the worst since 2015 and third since 2003, behind 2015 and 2006, though its range overlaps 2004. October 2026 alone was 3.8× its historical median. A naive splice of raw counts would have called 2026 a record; the harmonized record shows it was severe but not unprecedented. The calendar also reproduces the known August–October fire season and the large El Niño years (2006, 2015, 2019, 2023).

Local impact for Malaysia. Haze in Malaysia comes largely from fires across the Strait of Malacca in Sumatra and in Kalimantan. PyroSync includes presets for the main source provinces (Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, and West, Central and South Kalimantan). Local agencies, schools, journalists and residents can check within seconds whether the fires behind a haze episode are truly unusual, compared with a fair 20-year baseline, instead of relying on raw counts that exaggerate recent years.

Usability and accessibility.

  • One page, no sign-in.
  • A plain-language headline ranks the current season as soon as the page opens.
  • A colour-blind-safe cividis scale, with every chart labelled in words, not colour alone.
  • A “Why harmonize?” chart that shows users the false trend naive merging creates.

Limitations.

  • Thick smoke and cloud hide fires from both sensors, so the worst haze weeks may be under-counted.
  • Smouldering peat fires are partly missed even by VIIRS.
  • Harmonized values are estimates with a range, not measurements.
  • The most recent months use near-real-time data.
  • The calendar measures detected burning activity, not burned area.

How We Used Space Agency Data

All fire data comes from NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), downloaded through the FIRMS Archive Download for Indonesia, November 2000 to 14 November 2026:

In total we processed 7.8 million detections. We used the FIRMS fields for:

  • location, date and day/night pass, to build fire cell-days;
  • detection confidence, to filter quality;
  • the hotspot “type” flag, to remove volcanoes and static heat sources;
  • fire radiative power, as a machine-learning feature.

Standard-processing data is used where available, and near-real-time data for the most recent months. The FIRMS Active Fire Data Attributes documentation guided every field we used.

  • Tools and libraries: Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Plotly, PyArrow, GitHub Codespaces, Streamlit Community Cloud; map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors and CARTO (all listed in the Other Data field).
  • Background: Schroeder et al. (2014), The New VIIRS 375 m active fire detection data product; NASA NTRS, El Niño and fire activity in Indonesia, 2012–2024.
